### Option 1: Elevated & Literary (Preserves the evocative, artistic style while enhancing flow and mechanics)

What did he truly do, except lie beneath a pear tree wrapped in a heavy cloak, contemplating the motion of the heavenly bodies? *"Venerable,"* whispered the good citizens of Baltimore, their awe tinged with shock and a quiet dread. Rumor had it that he was given to strong drink—for how else could one explain his lingering beneath the night sky until dawn, or his solitary, unmarried state? 

Yet who could have been his match? Belonging to no simple category—neither Ethiopian nor English, neither uniquely fortunate nor entirely mad—he was like a vast, humming bird, mentally composing another impassioned letter to President Jefferson while anticipating a response that would be both polite and rhetorical. Travelers returning from Philadelphia recounted stories of the statue of Benjamin Franklin outside the library, rendered in his exact likeness and stature. A wife? *No, thank you.* 

At break of day, he milked the cows, returned indoors, and set a pot to stew while he slept. Nearby, the wooden clock he had whittled as a youth continued its faithful ticking. Neighbors would rouse him with gifts of warm bread and quilts. Then, as nightfall descended, he would venture out with his rifle—a striking, white-maned figure traversing the darkened heart of the Union—and aim toward the heavens, until, by some chance, a star seemed to go out. 

Had he taken a life? *“I assure thee, my dear Sir!”* Lowering his gaze to fields fragrant with the rich decay of spring, he could envision the nation’s domed capital rising from the surrounding morass, expanding outward in a brilliant spiral of lights.

---

### Option 2: Formal & Professional (Best for an essay, biography, or smooth narrative)

What occupied his days, other than resting beneath a pear tree wrapped in a great cloak, meditating upon the stars? *"Venerable,"* the locals of Baltimore whispered, filled with a mixture of shock and apprehension. It was rumored that he was prone to heavy drinking; how else to account for his standing under the stars all night, or his decision never to marry? 

Yet who would have suited him? He fit no easy definition—neither strictly Ethiopian nor English, neither exceptionally lucky nor insane. He was a creature of vast thought, mentally drafting another impassioned letter to President Jefferson while anticipating a polite, purely rhetorical reply. Those who had traveled to Philadelphia described the grand statue of Benjamin Franklin standing before the library, sculpted to his precise size and likeness. A wife? He preferred his solitude.

At dawn, he tended to the cows, then went inside to set a pot on the hearth before sleeping. Beside him, the wooden clock he had carved as a boy was still running. In the afternoons, thoughtful neighbors awakened him with fresh bread and quilts. At dusk, he emerged once more with his rifle—a white-maned silhouette moving across the darkened landscape of the young nation—and fired into the night sky until a star vanished from sight. 

Had he struck something down? *“I assure thee, my dear Sir!”* Looking down upon fields sweet with the scent of spring, he envisioned a new government’s domed city rising from the marshland, illuminating the night in a widening spiral of light.

---

To the tobacco farmers and mill hands along the muddy banks of the Patapsco, Benjamin was an enigma carved out of shadow—and shadow, in Baltimore County in the final decade of the eighteenth century, was something to be policed. They watched his dark, weathered cabin from a distance, whispering behind their cupped hands. They spoke of a free Black man who slept while the sun burned high, who kept no livestock, and whose hearth fire cast unnatural, flickering silhouettes late into the dark. Some whispered of sorcery; others, of sedition. They could comprehend a man bent double over a hoe under a midday sun, but they could not comprehend a mind that inhabited the night.

Inside the cabin, safe behind a heavy oak door barred against the world’s mistrust, Benjamin existed in a universe governed by absolute precision. 

The heart of his sanctuary was a clock. Forty years prior, using borrowed books and a pocket watch as his only guides, he had carved every gear, pin, and pendulum out of seasoned American cedar with a small penknife. Decades later, its wooden teeth still meshed seamlessly, striking the hours with a deep, resonant chime that echoed the pulse of the quiet room. 

Around the clock lay the tools of a quiet revolution: brass dividers, a reflecting telescope, ink-stained sheets of parchment covered in logarithmic tables, and meticulously drafted ephemerides tracking the paths of the moon and stars. 

When the village sank into sleep, Benjamin’s day began. He stepped out onto his porch, pulling a woolen coat against the night chill. He pointed his telescope toward the heavens, seeking solace in the indifferent, perfect geometry of the cosmos. Up there, in the transit of Venus and the steady wheel of the constellations, was a truth uncorrupted by human cruelty. The stars did not ask for the color of the observer's skin; they merely demanded the rigor of his calculations.

Yet, even as his eyes traced the celestial equator, his mind remained tethered to the earth, churning with a quiet, righteous fury. 

For months, he had been mentally composing a letter. It was an epistle addressed to the primary architect of American liberty: Thomas Jefferson, then Secretary of State. As Benjamin adjusted the focus of his lens, he polished the sentences in his head, sharpening each phrase like a scalpel. 

*Sir,* his mind rehearsed, *how can you, who penned the self-evident truth that all men are created equal, continue to hold your brothers in a state of groaning servitude? How can the same intellect that measured the light of freedom justify the darkness imposed upon my brethren?*

He did not intend to write as a beggar asking for a favor, but as an intellectual equal demanding a reconciliation between the nation’s noble creed and its tragic reality. He would send Jefferson his own hand-calculated astronomical almanac as irreputable proof that the mind knows no racial bounds.

As the hour neared three in the morning, the wooden clock inside struck with a solemn ring. Benjamin closed his eyes, resting his brow against the cool metal of the telescope. Weariness washed over him, and in the space between waking and dreaming, the night air seemed to thicken, heavy with the scent of river mud and rotting vegetation.

A vision unfolded before his closed eyes, vivid and haunting.

He saw a vast, suffocating swamp along the banks of the Potomac—a dark wilderness of reeds, fog, and mire, desolate and formless. But as he watched, lines of glowing light cut through the gloom. They were surveyor’s chains, sights set through transit levels, precise geometric axes drawn directly from the stars he had just been mapping. 

Up from the mud, guided by those unseen, perfect lines, rose the grand skeleton of a national capital. Classical columns pierced the fog. Wide, sweeping avenues cleaved through the thickets. And at the center of it all, crowning a high hill that crested above the marsh, a great, domed building rose toward the heavens—a shining pantheon dedicated to liberty.

Benjamin looked closer at the foundation of this luminous city. Deep beneath the marble, beneath the grand plazas and the soaring dome, were the hands that had laid the stakes, the minds that had calculated the boundary lines, and the bruised bodies of the forgotten who had cleared the brush. The grand city did not spring from the ground by the grace of statesmen alone; it was anchored in the soil by the silent, unacknowledged labor and genius of the marginalized.

The vision faded, leaving Benjamin alone in the cool Baltimore night, the damp breeze rustling the leaves of his modest garden. 

He opened his eyes. The sky in the east was beginning to soften into a pale, pearlescent gray. Down in the valley, the first roosters began to crow, and his neighbors would soon awaken, still suspecting him of darkness, completely blind to the light he harbored.

Benjamin stepped back inside his cabin. He walked over to his desk, lit a fresh candle, and dipped his quill into the inkstand. The time for mental rehearsal was over. As his cedar clock ticked away the precious seconds of a fledgling nation's youth, the isolated polymath began to write, his hand steady, charting the long, painful transit of a country toward its promised light.

**What** defines the true soul of a city? Is it the silhouette of its skyline against the harbor, the rhythm of its neighborhood streets, or the quiet weight of the history etched into its stone? In **Baltimore**, Maryland, the answer lies in a rich tapestry of resilience, faith, and historic firsts that have earned the city a uniquely **venerable** place in the American story.

Long known as "Charm City," Baltimore holds a distinguished position as the cradle of American Catholicism. As the nation’s first archdiocese—often called the "Premier See"—it served as the spiritual anchor for a young country finding its footing. Yet, beyond the grand architecture of the Baltimore Basilica, the city’s most **venerable** legacy rests in the courage of the individuals who walked its streets and fought for justice long before the world was ready to grant it.

Chief among these figures is Mother Mary Lange, an Afro-Cuban immigrant who arrived in **Baltimore** in the early 19th century. In a city where slavery was still legal and systemic prejudice was rampant, Lange recognized a desperate need for the education of Black youth. With steadfast devotion, she established the Oblate Sisters of Providence in 1829—the first religious order for women of African descent in the Catholic Church. 

Decades of quiet dedication followed, as the order provided education, shelter, and care to the marginalized. In June 2023, the Vatican officially declared Mother Mary Lange to be **Venerable**, a significant step toward canonization that acknowledges her heroic virtue and selfless life. Her legacy is a testament to **what** can be accomplished when faith meets unflinching resolve in the face of adversity.

So, **what** makes Baltimore truly **venerable**? It is not merely the passage of time or the age of its historic ports. It is the enduring spirit of leaders like Mother Mary Lange and the generations of Baltimoreans who have chosen hope over hardship. Through its deep roots, transformative history, and commitment to uplifting all its citizens, **Baltimore** continues to offer a compelling answer to **what** it means to leave a lasting, sacred mark on the world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a vivid, lyrical vignette about Benjamin Banneker living in Maryland, blending local rumors about his stargazing and solitude with his internal thoughts about his wooden clock, his letter to Thomas Jefferson, and the new capital city being built.
counterfactuals.output:
In the steep, oak-shadowed hollows near Ellicott’s Mills, the locals spoke of Benjamin Banneker in hushed, uncertain tones. To the farmers and millhands, the old recluse was an enigma wrapped in a wool cloak, a man who seemed to trade sleep with the devil for the secrets of the sky. They whispered at the tavern that he lay flat on his back in his cabin yard all night, staring through a long brass tube, counting the pale teeth of the moon while honest men slept. Some called him a wizard; others, a foolish hermit who drank the night air until his blood turned to shadow.

Inside the cabin, safe from their whispers, the room breathed with a singular, steady pulse. 

*Tick-clack. Tick-clack.*

It was not the sharp, cold click of brass or iron, but the deep, resonant heartbeat of cherry wood. Benjamin sat at his pine table, his hand resting near the wooden clock he had whittled half a century ago. Every gear, tooth, and axle had been carved from his own youth with a simple pocketknife, guided by the guts of a borrowed pocket watch he had memorized and returned. For fifty years, without missing a strike, the wooden throat of the clock had chimed the hours. 

He smiled, feeling the faint vibration through the timber of his desk. *I carved time out of a tree,* he thought, his thumb trailing over a map of the heavens. *If a Black man can trap the invisible river of time in a block of Maryland cedar, how can they say his soul was forged without reason?*

His eyes drifted to the copy of the letter resting beside his brass quadrant—the letter he had sent across the miles to Thomas Jefferson, then Secretary of State. The ink felt hot even now, months after it had been dispatched alongside his manuscript almanac. He remembered the precise weight of the words he had hurled like stones against the high glass windows of the statesman’s philosophy: *Sir, suffer me to recall to your mind that time in which the arms and authority of the British Crown were exerted...*

How carefully Mr. Jefferson wrote of liberty, yet how comfortably he kept men in chains! Benjamin’s chest tightened with the memory of his own daring. He had forced the author of the Declaration of Independence to look into the mirror of his own hypocrisy. Jefferson’s reply had been polite, smooth as polished marble, yet cool as cellar ice. But Benjamin knew the mathematical truth of things: a line was either straight or it was crooked. Slavery was a monstrous bend in the geometry of a young nation, and no polished prose could make it true.

Beyond his shuttered window, far down the muddy banks of the Potomac, that nation was carving its new heart out of the wilderness. Benjamin closed his eyes and saw it clearly—the Federal City. He could still feel the chill of the morning mists from his months spent surveying the marshy territory with Major Ellicott. Through the lens of his transit instrument, Benjamin had helped pull down the stars to fix the precise corners of the new capital. He had mapped the avenues where presidents would walk, holding the grand grid of Washington in his mind when others saw only brush, thicket, and enslaved men hauling stone. 

They were building a city of light on a foundation of shadows. 

A bird called outside, a faint herald of the approaching dawn. The night was folding its dark velvet velvet back toward the western horizon, swallowing the constellations—Orion, the Pleiades, the precise celestial pathways he had mapped in his almanac to save sailors and guide farmers.

Let the neighbors whisper that he was a madman or a creature of the dark. Let the grand architects of the republic forget the old sable philosopher who had laid down their first lines in the mud. Benjamin Banneker dipped his quill in black ink, adjusted his spectacles, and leaned over his ledger. 

The cherry-wood clock struck four, a warm, resonant chime echoing through the small cabin. It was the sound of a artfully measured universe, keeping perfect time, waiting patiently for the rest of the world to catch up.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of atmospheric historical fiction about an early American polymath that captures the surreal feeling of watching a new nation take shape from a quiet farm at night.
counterfactuals.output:
The wooden clock he had carved by hand forty years ago beat its steady, dry rhythm into the dark. *Tick. Clack. Tick.* It was a lone heart thumping inside the log cabin, measuring time that felt, on nights like this, entirely unmoored from the earth.

Benjamin Banneker stepped onto the threshold, his wool cloak pulled tight against the late-autumn chill of the Maryland hills. Below his tobacco field, the Patapsco River was invisible, recognizable only by the cold, damp mist rising through the timber. 

He set his brass transit on its wooden tripod, the brass cool against his calloused fingertips. 

To the south, thirty miles through oak forest and marsh, men were sleeping in tents along the Potomac. Earlier that year, Benjamin had walked those lowlands beside Andrew Ellicott, sighting through lenses, measuring zenith distances, laying down the boundary lines for a city that did not yet exist. The Federal District. A capital for a republic built of ink, rhetoric, and swamp mud. 

Out here, under the vault of the ecliptic, the nation felt less like an empire and more like a phantom. 

He leaned into the eyepiece. The heavens were indifferent and exact. Jupiter hung bright near the meridian, flanked by the pinpoint pearls of its Galilean moons. Benjamin adjusted the thumb-screw, watching the small, pale spheres drift across his hairline grid. He noted the time on his slate, calculating the ephemeris for his upcoming almanac. 

It was a strange thing, he thought, dipping his quill into the ink-horn on the stump beside him, to watch a world invent itself in the dark. 

For a hundred years, this continent had been a wilderness of trees and silver rivers, carved into royal grants and quiet plantations. Now, in the tavern parlors of Philadelphia and the brick houses of Annapolis, men spoke of "The Great Experiment" as though they were alchemists turning lead into light. They debated constitutions and bill of rights while the crickets sang the same cadence they had sung for ten thousand years.

Just over the western ridge, a dog barked once, its sound swallowed immediately by the vast, black canopy of pine and chest-nut. Somewhere past that ridge lay thousands of miles of unbroken forest, stretching toward rivers no white man had mapped, under stars no philosopher had named. And yet, on paper, it was all being claimed. Lines were being drawn across the dark. A democracy was being spoken into the void, fragile as glass, forged by men who wrote of universal liberty while their enslaved hands plowed the very soil beneath his feet.

Benjamin looked at his own hands—dark, weathered, stained with walnut juice and India ink. A free Black man sitting on a solitary farm, predicting the movements of the moon for farmers who would never look him in the eye. 

He looked back down his transit scope. The stars moved with majestic, unyielding geometry. Up there, order reigned. Down here, a nation was taking shape like a ship being assembled in the dark—planks groaning, iron pins being hammered into raw timber, floating on an uncharted sea. 

He took a slow breath, inhaling the scent of damp earth, woodsmoke, and dying leaves. 

The clock inside struck two, its wooden gears clicking with a dry, soft rasp. Benjamin wiped his slate clean, picked up his brass instrument, and turned back toward his lit candle. Tomorrow the sun would rise over a country that was still mostly an idea, but tonight, on a quiet hill in Oella, he had seen it moving in the dark, spinning wildly around the sun.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine Benjamin Banneker's daily life through the eyes of a literary narrator. Include details about his pear tree, his handmade clock, the gossip of his Baltimore neighbors, and his imaginary dialogs with Thomas Jefferson.
counterfactuals.output:
The day did not begin for Benjamin Banneker with the crowing of a cock or the first graying of the Maryland sky, but with the measured, wooden heartbeat of his own creation. 

Inside the small, timber cabin tucked into the hills of Oella, the clock struck five. It was a marvel carved fifty years prior—every gear, wheel, and pendulum shaped from white oak with nothing more than a pocketknife and a borrowed pocket watch for a blueprint. It had not missed a beat in half a century. To Benjamin, now an old man with wool-white hair and hands stained with ink, the clock was not merely a keeper of hours; it was proof that order could be wrought from raw, silent wood, just as a mind could carve truth from the chaos of the wilderness.

He stepped outside into the crisp morning air, his joints stiff from a night spent hunched over astronomical tables. He walked toward the ancient pear tree that stood like a sentinel beside his door. Its roots drank deep from the red soil; its branches bowed low, heavy with hard, green fruit that smelled of rain and cold honey. Benjamin plucked a pear, feeling its rough skin against his thumb, and bit into it. The sweetness was sharp, grounding him. Under this canopy, he was neither a freedman bound by the unspoken anxieties of a slaveholding state nor a curiosity to be gawkily admired. He was simply a man partaking in the quiet arithmetic of the seasons.

Down the winding dirt track that led toward Baltimore, the world was waking up, and with it, the whispers. 

Benjamin could hear the faint rumble of tobacco wagons heading toward the port, and he knew what was said when the drivers passed his gate. The tavern keepers and smallholders of Baltimore County spoke of the "sable astronomer" in tones that wavered between superstitious dread and reluctant awe. 

*"He stays up all night staring through a long glass at the moon,"* a farmer’s wife would murmur over her wash-tub. 
*"Leaves his land untended while he plays with numbers,"* a merchant would scoff. 
*"They say he can foretell an eclipse. Is it God’s work, or witchcraft? How does a Negro know the architecture of the heavens when he was meant for the plow?"*

Benjamin knew these rumors. They blew through the trees like dry leaves. He did not fight them; he simply let them drift past his porch. Their ignorance was a fog, but his geometry was sunlight. 

Returning to his cabin, he sat at his pine table, moving aside the brass brass quadrant and the tallow candles. Before him lay his ephemeris—pages covered in the fine, dark spiders of his handwriting, calculating the exact movements of the sun, moon, and planets for his upcoming almanac. 

And there, sitting in the empty chair across from him, was Thomas Jefferson.

The Secretary of State was not physically in the room, of course, but his ghost sat permanent residence in Benjamin’s mind. Ever since Benjamin had dispatched his famous letter to Monticello—alongside a handwritten copy of his almanac—their imaginary dialogue had never truly ceased.

*“You see, Mr. Jefferson,”* Benjamin murmured aloud, his quiet voice blending with the steady *tick-clack* of the wooden clock, *“you wrote that all men are created equal. An elegant phrase. A noble posture. Yet you hold human beings in chains and ponder whether my people possess a capacity for reason.”*

He dipped his quill into the inkhorn, the feather trembling slightly in his aged hand.

*In your mind, sir,* Benjamin continued, staring at the empty air where the statesman’s polished silhouette rested, *you imagine us as creatures of instinct, devoid of the higher arts. But look at this table. Look at these numbers. The moon does not care about the color of the hand that calculates her orbit. She moves by law. Does God grant the white man the sun and leave the Black man only the night? Or did He give us both the intellect to measure them?*

He imagined Jefferson shifting uncomfortably, adjusting his fine linen cuffs, offering the slick, cautious evasions of a politician-philosopher. *“It is an experiment, Mr. Banneker,”* the ghost would reply. *“A matter of time.”*

*“Time?”* Benjamin whispered, his eyes flicking to the wooden clock. *“Time is the very thing you steal from us. Every hour a man spends under the lash is an hour he cannot spend looking at the stars.”*

A breeze blew through the open window, carrying the scent of crushed pear leaves and damp earth. The ghost dissolved into the dusty sunbeams, but the argument remained, burning bright and cold within Benjamin’s chest. 

He looked down at his parchment. The numbers were clear. A solar eclipse was coming. He had calculated the hour, the minute, the second. He would publish it, and the white men of Baltimore, Philadelphia, and Monticello would look to the sky at the precise moment he dictated, and they would see the sun eclipsed by a truth they could no longer deny.

Outside, the sun climbed higher, warming the pear tree. Inside, the wooden clock struck twelve, its tones rich and resonant, echoing through the quiet house. Benjamin Banneker took up his glass, turned his face toward the light, and went back to work.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem inspired by the life and mythos of Benjamin Banneker, focusing on his night-owl stargazing habits, his isolation as a free Black intellectual, and his vision of Washington D.C. rising from the swamp.
counterfactuals.output:
When the county folded into the dark, Benjamin let the sun—that harsh, revealing lamp of plantation labor and pale overseers—sink beneath the Maryland pines. Night was his true republic, cool and unpigmented. In his cabin, the wooden clock he had carved with a pocketknife fifty years before ticked its dry, cedar beat, a heart wrought from timber, while above his skylight the darkness opened its vault of unassailable geometry. Through the lens of his brass telescope, the heavens were not a mystery but a ledger. He tracked the silver drift of Jupiter, calculated the precise, terrifying shadow of an eclipse before it fell, and found in the quiet depth of three in the morning a sanctuary where a Black man’s mind was as infinite as the vacuum between the stars.

Yet his liberty was an island bounded by a sea of iron and rope. To be free, self-taught, and brilliant in a land that deemed his flesh a commodity was a peculiar, heavy solitude. White gentlemen marvelled at his existence as if he were a lightning bolt caught in a jar, while his enslaved brothers in the nearby fields carried a grief he could only watch from his window. He was a singular human constellation, suspended in the chill air between two worlds—too vast for the cage built for his skin, too alone to find a peer among the living. When he sat to write his almanacs, he dipped his quill into an ink that burned with quiet defiance, addressing his calculations to Thomas Jefferson like a lantern thrust into a deep, national fog, proving with every predicted tide that the soul has no color, only velocity and light.

And when they called him to the malarial marshes along the Potomac, he brought the heavens down to the mud. While others bickered over horse-trading and boundaries, Benjamin lay on his back in the damp midnight brush, his eye pressed to the transit, holding the spinning earth still against the fixed point of a star. Out of the thicket and the frog-song, out of the dark, sucking rot of the swamp, he drew the invisible grid of the future city. He mapped the grand avenues through the wilderness, sighting the north star to anchor the nation’s central axis, reconstructing from memory and stellar math the blueprint of power before a single marble block was quarried. 

He saw it all rising from the muck—monuments springing from the Black mire, a city of freedom charted by a man denied its promise. Long after his cabin burned to cinders, long after his wooden clock melted into ash, the avenues of the capital still reach toward the constellations he summoned down into the wild. He remains there, buried in the foundation of the federal grid: the midnight scholar who looked past the shadows of a young, hypocritical nation and laid its sightlines straight against the sky.

counterfactuals.prompt: "Neither Ethiopian nor English, neither lucky nor crazy"—write a surreal flash fiction piece about a 18th-century Black astronomer who shoots at the stars and dreams of the nation's new domed capital.
counterfactuals.output:
Jeremiah set his heels into the cold Potomac mud, the surveyor’s brass chain coiled at his hip like a sleeping viper. In his left hand he held an ivory quadrant; in his right, an iron flintlock pistol packed with silver shot and pulverized slate. 

High above the salt-marsh, the 18th century lay stretched across the night, vast and unmapped. 

When the white commissioners in the timber-framed taverns asked where his lineage was anchored, Jeremiah refused the tidy boxes of their ledgers. *Neither Ethiopian nor English,* he told the dark water, adjusting his sight against the pale throat of Orion. *Neither lucky nor crazy.* He was merely a creature of the meridian, a man made entirely of geometry and gunpowder, standing on the rim of an unhatched world.

He raised the pistol to the zenith and pulled the trigger. 

*Flash. Sulfur.* 

The bullet did not fall back down. High above the marsh, a dull *clink* reverberated through the dark—the sound of lead striking a curved ceiling. Where the shot hit between Betelgeuse and Rigel, a tiny spiderweb crack bloomed in the night sky. A fine, luminous powder drifted down, smelling of wet lime and hot marble. 

Jeremiah caught the falling star-dust on his palm and rubbed it between his thumb and forefinger. It was the mortar of the unborn world. 

In his mind, and on the pigskin parchment weighted down by river stones at his feet, the nation’s new capital was already rising out of the reeds. It was not a city of wood and pig-pens, but a fever dream of perfect circles. At its center stood the Dome—a colossal, blinding rotunda of whitewashed stone, smooth as an ostrich egg, designed to trap the light of the sun and hold it hostage. 

He loaded the pistol again. A second shot struck the bell of the sky. *Clink.* Another fissure opened, dropping a flake of blue-white ether into the mud. 

With every bullet he fired into the heavens, Jeremiah shaved a fraction of an inch off the firmament, bringing the sky down to earth. He was not trying to slay the stars; he was harvesting them. He was stealing the vault of heaven to build the ceiling of the state. 

He envisioned the men who would one day sit beneath that vast, vaulted plaster, debating liberty in linen cravats, entirely unaware that their magnificent dome was held together by the shattered glass of the constellations, calculated by a man whose skin they would only ever measure in terms of property.

The wind shifted, carrying the sound of distant broadaxes echoing from the woods where the new city’s avenues were being cleared. They were cutting down the oaks, but Jeremiah was mapping the shadows. 

He aimed at the North Star—the anchor, the fixed pivot of slaves and sailors. 

"Neither Ethiopian nor English," Jeremiah whispered, his voice disappearing into the fog. "Only the architect."

He pulled the trigger. The universe rang like a struck goblet, and for a fraction of a second, the swamp was illuminated by the blinding, impossible silhouette of a white capital floating in the dark, grand and hollow, waiting to be lived in.
